thought_title: Unity with the bishop as unity with God
orientation: Ignatius is writing to the church in Ephesus, urging them to remain united around their bishop, elders, and deacons, and now grounds this in his own brief but spiritual bond with their bishop Onesimus.
pass_a_gloss: For if I in [a] small time such [a] closeness had toward the bishop of you, not human being, but spiritual, how much more [do] I call you blessed, the [ones] mixed together thus, as the church [is mixed] [with] Jesus Christ, and as Jesus Christ [is mixed] [with] the Father, so that all things in unity [may be] harmonious? Let no one be deceived: if anyone is not within the altar, he is deprived of the bread of God. For if of one and [of a] second [person] prayer such strength has, how much more [does] the [prayer] of the bishop and of [the] whole church? The [one] therefore not coming to the same [place], this [one] already is arrogant and himself has separated. For it is written: 'To [the] arrogant God opposes [himself].' Let us be eager therefore not to oppose [ourselves] to the bishop, so that we may be [ones] submitting [ourselves] to God.

lemmas.gloss: let us be eager, make every effort

choices.why: The noun denotes an intimate, habitual bond; 'closeness' captures the relational warmth without implying mere habit or custom.
The perfect participle of 'mix together' suggests a stable, blended union; 'closely united' conveys the ongoing state rather than a one-time mixing.
The phrase is a fixed idiom for the gathered congregation; 'common assembly' makes the communal gathering explicit for modern readers.
The verb denotes active prideful behavior; 'is arrogant' keeps the present-tense state of pride that leads to separation.
The aorist of 'separate' with the reflexive pronoun indicates self-separation from the community; 'has cut himself off' preserves the reflexive force and completed action.

pass_b_english: If I could enjoy such closeness with your bishop in so short a time, a closeness not merely human but spiritual, how much more do I count you blessed, who are as closely united with him as the church is with Jesus Christ, and as Jesus Christ is with the Father, so that all things may be in harmonious unity?

Let no one be deceived: if anyone is not within the altar, he is deprived of the bread of God. For if the prayer of one or two has such power, how much more does the prayer of the bishop and of the whole church?

So the one who does not come to the common assembly is already arrogant and has cut himself off. For it is written: "God opposes the arrogant" (Proverbs 3:34). Let us be eager, then, not to oppose the bishop, so that we may be subject to God.
